kurals.tamil:
துணைநலம் ஆக்கம் தரூஉம் வினைநலம்
வேண்டிய எல்லாந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thunainalam aakkam tharooum vinainalam
Vendiya ellaan tharum.
kurals.meaning: Good allies can bring a person increase and wealth, but goodness in the deeds themselves brings everything one could wish for.
kurals.elementary: Good friends can help you build a bigger sandcastle. But if you build it the right way, patiently and fairly, you get the castle, you keep your friends, and people want to play with you again. Doing things the right way gives you more than any helper can.
kurals.university: The chapter opens by ranking two kinds of nalam (goodness, excellence): tuṇai-nalam, the excellence of one’s supporters, the theme of the earlier chapter on seeking the help of the great (ch. 45), and vinai-nalam, the goodness or purity of the action itself, which gives the chapter its name, vinai-t-tūymai. Parimelazhagar reads ākkam narrowly as material increase, while vēṇṭiya ellām (all that is desired) takes in fame and merit in this world and the next, so good allies secure only one good while pure action secures all of them. The line sets the ethical frame for this part of the Amaichiyal (chapters on the minister, 64-73): a minister’s competence (ch. 64) and eloquence (ch. 65) are worthless unless the means he uses are clean. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah follow this contrast closely, while Kalaignar softens it into a partnership in which allies add strength and good deeds done with them bring every benefit. On the text: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both print த்ருஉம், an evident keying error. The sandhi-joined text at thirukkural-thamizh.org has தரூஉம் (tarūum, the alapeṭai lengthening of tarum), and that reading is adopted here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “By worship of the Lord, who is the source of all beings and who is all-pervading, a man can attain perfection through performing his own work.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna teaches that one’s own duty, rightly done and offered to God, is itself the path to perfection; nothing outside the right action is needed.
hinduism.tie_back: Like vinai-nalam, rightly performed action is the source from which every good end follows.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 18.46 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea that right action yields the highest good, but the Gita frames it devotionally rather than as a contrast with allies.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells his hearers to put righteousness first and trust that the material needs they worry about will follow.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts say that putting rightness first brings ‘all these things’ along with it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close structural parallel (right conduct first, everything else follows), though Matthew speaks of the kingdom of God, not statecraft.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while he is a believer - We will surely cause him to live a good life, and We will surely give them their reward [in the Hereafter] according to the best of what they used to do.”
islam.explanation: The Quran promises that righteous action brings a good life now and the best reward later.
islam.tie_back: Righteous deeds yielding both this-worldly and next-worldly good match Parimelazhagar’s gloss of ‘all that is desired’.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on good action yielding every kind of good; lacks the Kural’s contrast with allies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Study is not the most important thing, but actions”
judaism.explanation: Shimon ben Gamaliel sums up a lifetime among the sages: what counts in the end is not learning or talk but deeds.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise puts the quality of the deed above every outside aid.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the primacy of the deed, but Avot contrasts deeds with study rather than with allies.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada opens by teaching that action from a pure mind brings happiness that never leaves the doer.
buddhism.tie_back: Pure action (tūymai) as the thing that brings every good matches the Kural’s vinai-nalam.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on purity of action bringing lasting good; the Buddhist stress is on the mind behind the act.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Prodicus’ fable, told by Socrates in Xenophon, the young Heracles meets Virtue and Vice at a crossroads, and Virtue tells him the gods give nothing truly good without toil and right effort.
greek_mythology.explanation: Vice offers an easy road to pleasure; Virtue promises real goods, honour, friends and a blessed name, only through honest labour.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the myth says the right way of acting, not easy help, wins everything worth having.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good thematic match on the right path yielding all goods; the fable is about personal choice, not a minister’s means.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that at the Olympic Games the crown goes not to the finest or strongest onlookers but to those who compete, and in the same way it is those who act rightly who win the noble and good things in life.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle happiness is found in virtuous activity itself, not in possessions or outside advantages.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural too puts the quality of the action ahead of outside supports.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Parallel on excellent activity as the source of the good life; Aristotle does grant that external goods are needed too.

kurals.tamil:
என்றும் ஒருவுதல் வேண்டும் புகழொடு
நன்றி பயவா வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Endrum oruvudhal vendum pugazhodu
Nandri payavaa vinai.
kurals.meaning: At all times one must give up any deed that brings neither honour nor real good.
kurals.elementary: Before you do something, ask two questions: will people be proud of me for this, and will it truly help? If the answer to both is no, don’t do it, even if it looks easy or tempting.
kurals.university: The couplet gives the test that runs through the whole chapter: a deed must yield pukaḻ (fame, good name) together with naṉṟi (benefit, goodness), and a deed that yields neither is to be avoided (oruvutal, ‘setting aside, shunning’) at all times (eṉṟum). Parimelazhagar and later commentators such as Solomon Pappaiah read the pair as fame in this life and merit (aṟam) for the life to come, so a clean act must be both publicly honourable and morally fruitful. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the rejected deeds as those ‘without purity’ (tūymai aṟṟa), tying the verse to the chapter title. The prose explanation printed with Pope’s translation (‘acts which, in addition to fame, yield no benefit’) reads pukaḻoṭu slightly differently, but all readings agree that honour alone is not enough without real good. The text is stable across all three sources consulted.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu tells the householder to avoid the pursuit of wealth and pleasure whenever they conflict with dharma, the sacred law.
hinduism.explanation: The lawgiver ranks artha (wealth) and kāma (desire) below dharma and tells the householder to give up any gain that goes against it.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, Manu rules out any act that does not also serve the good, however profitable it looks.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close match on renouncing gain and action that lack dharmic worth; paraphrased, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report; if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the Philippians to fix their minds on what is both morally good and of good report.
christianity.tie_back: Paul’s pairing of virtue and praise mirrors the Kural’s pairing of naṉṟi and pukaḻ.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same double test of goodness and good report, but Paul is shaping thought, not ruling out actions.

islam.quote_or_event: “Wealth and children are [but] adornment of the worldly life. But the enduring good deeds are better to your Lord for reward and better for [one’s] hope.”
islam.explanation: The Quran sets passing worldly gains against good deeds whose worth lasts.
islam.tie_back: The Kural too tells the doer to choose only deeds whose good lasts beyond the moment.
islam._accuracy_note: Shares the preference for lasting good over passing gain; the Kural’s explicit fame test is missing.

judaism.quote_or_event: “which is the straight path that a man should choose for himself? One which is an honor to the person adopting it, and [on account of which] honor [accrues] to him from others.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Judah the Prince defines the right path as one that is honourable in itself and also brings honour from other people.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost exactly the Kural’s double test: a deed must be good in itself and bring an honourable name.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close structural parallel of inner worth and public honour as the test of a course of action.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Vanijja Sutta the Buddha names five trades a lay follower should not practise: dealing in weapons, in living beings, in meat, in intoxicants and in poisons.
buddhism.explanation: These livelihoods may be profitable, but they cause harm, so a disciple is told to give them up entirely.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the sutta rules out whole kinds of action because they bring no real good, however much they earn.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Good match on giving up profitable but harmful work; the sutta names specific trades rather than stating a general test.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod warns his brother Perses that the road to badness is smooth and close at hand, while the gods have set sweat before goodness, on a road that is long and steep at first but easy once the top is reached.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet urges choosing the harder path that leads to real worth over the easy one that leads to ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural too asks for the discipline to turn down easy acts that bring no honour and no good.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Broad thematic parallel on choosing the worthy path; Hesiod does not give the double fame-and-good test.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Cicero argues that nothing can truly be expedient (utile) that is not also morally right (honestum), and that the appearance of profit in a wrong act is always a delusion.
philosophy.explanation: Book 3 of On Duties is built on the claim that the useful and the honourable can never really conflict.
philosophy.tie_back: Cicero’s refusal to separate profit from honour matches the Kural’s demand for deeds that bring both good name and good.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close conceptual parallel, also written as advice for statesmen.

kurals.tamil:
ஒஓதல் வேண்டும் ஒளிமாழ்கும் செய்வினை
ஆஅதும் என்னு மவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oodhal vendum olimaazhkum seyvinai
Aaadhum ennu mavar.
kurals.meaning: Those who say ‘we shall rise higher’ must avoid any deed that would dim the light of their good name.
kurals.elementary: If you want to become class captain, you wouldn’t cheat on a test, because once people see you cheat they stop trusting you. Anyone who wants to grow greater has to keep their good name bright and stay away from anything that would spoil it.
kurals.university: Two alapeṭai (metrical lengthenings) mark the couplet: ஒஓதல் for ஓதல்/ஒருவுதல் (avoiding, shunning), and ஆஅதும் for ஆதும், ‘we shall become (greater)’, which Parimelazhagar takes as the resolve of those who seek to rise ever higher. Oḷi (light, radiance) stands here for reputation and dignity, and oḷi-māḻkum seyviṉai means acts that cause that radiance to fade. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both take oḷi as pukaḻ (fame), linking this verse to the fame-and-good test of 652, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as ‘one’s standing in one’s own lifetime’. The logic is a statesman’s: ambition itself is a reason for scruple, since a stained name blocks the rise one hopes for. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined form ஒஓதல் வேண்டு மொளிமாழ்குஞ் செய்வினை / யாஅது மென்னு மவர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “People will always speak of your infamy, and for a respectable person, dishonor is worse than death.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna warns Arjuna that deserting his duty would bring lasting disgrace, which for a man of standing is worse than dying.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts treat a dimmed name as a loss too great for someone who aims high to risk.
hinduism.source: Bhagavad Gita 2.34 (Prabhupada, Bhagavad-gita As It Is)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on protecting honour; the Gita’s context is battlefield duty rather than clean means in office.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.”
christianity.explanation: Peter tells scattered believers to live so honestly that even their critics will be won over by their good works.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, Peter treats blameless conduct as the guard of a good name that others are watching.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shared concern for reputation kept through clean conduct; the aim in Peter is God’s glory, not personal rise.

islam.quote_or_event: “Whoever desires honor [through power] - then to Allah belongs all honor. To Him ascends good speech, and righteous work raises it. But they who plot evil deeds will have a severe punishment, and the plotting of those - it will perish.”
islam.explanation: The verse tells those who seek honour that only righteous work truly raises a person, while scheming comes to nothing.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural closely: people who want to rise must hold to deeds that lift, not ones that disgrace.
islam._accuracy_note: Close match on the link between seeking honour, rising, and avoiding corrupt deeds.

judaism.quote_or_event: “There are three crowns: the crown of Torah, the crown of priesthood, and the crown of royalty, but the crown of a good name supersedes them all.”
judaism.explanation: Rabbi Shimon ranks a good name above even learning, priesthood and kingship.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural likewise treats a bright name as the thing an ambitious person must guard above all.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the supreme value of reputation; Avot does not explicitly link it to avoiding deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not the sweet smell of flowers, not even the fragrance of sandal, tagara, or jasmine blows against the wind. But the fragrance of the virtuous blows against the wind.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the reputation of the virtuous spreads in every direction, which no ordinary perfume can do.
buddhism.tie_back: The ‘fragrance’ of virtue is the Buddhist image for the same radiance (oḷi) that the Kural says wrong deeds would dim.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Parallel image of virtue’s radiance or fragrance; the verse praises virtue rather than warning against dimming it.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hector tells Andromache he would feel dire shame before the Trojan men and women if he shrank from battle like a coward, for he has learned always to stand among the foremost and win glory for his father and himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hector chooses danger over any act that would stain the honour he and his house have built.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s aspirant, Hector will not do what dims his name, whatever it costs him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on protecting honour; Homeric kleos is martial glory rather than a minister’s clean conduct.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle’s great-souled person (megalopsychos), who is concerned above all with honour, will not stoop to anything base or shameful, since honour is the greatest of external goods and is fitting only to the good.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle real honour can belong only to virtue, so one who seeks it cannot act basely.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s logic that the ambition to rise is itself a reason to avoid tarnishing deeds.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good conceptual fit on honour requiring virtue; Aristotle’s portrait is broader than the Kural’s single maxim.

kurals.tamil:
இடுக்கண் படினும் இளிவந்த செய்யார்
நடுக்கற்ற காட்சி யவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Idukkan padinum ilivandha seyyaar
Nadukkatra kaatchi yavar.
kurals.meaning: People of clear, unshaken understanding will not do anything shameful, even when they are in serious trouble.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you lost your lunch money and saw someone else’s wallet on the floor. A person with a steady, clear mind would still hand it in, even though they’re hungry. Being in trouble doesn’t make a wrong thing right.
kurals.university: Iṭukkaṇ is ‘distress, affliction’ (compare the chapter iṭukkaṇ aḻiyāmai, ch. 63), and iḷivanta means ‘what brings disgrace’. Parimelazhagar takes the past-tense participle literally as ‘acts that have (in the past) brought disgrace’, which is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘acts which have brought disgrace (on former ministers)’. The key phrase naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, ‘vision free of trembling’, describes firm, clear discernment that does not waver under pressure, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘motionless, clear knowledge’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar add that such people will not act basely even to escape their distress, which prepares for the stronger case of 656. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read இடுக்கண் படினும்; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi form இடுக்கட் படினு மிளிவந்த.

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, tested by the sage Vishvamitra, loses his kingdom, sells his wife and son, and works as a servant at a cremation ground, yet never breaks his word or his truthfulness.
hinduism.explanation: However deep his suffering, the king refuses to buy relief with a dishonourable act, and in the end the gods restore him.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the classic Indian example of the ‘unshaken vision’ that will not stoop even in great distress.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close narrative match; the legend is famous in Tamil tradition as well.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Choosing rather to suffer affliction with the people of God, than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a season;”
christianity.explanation: Hebrews praises Moses for choosing hardship with his people over the comforts of Pharaoh’s court.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s steady-minded person, Moses accepts affliction rather than take a dishonourable way out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel on preferring suffering to wrongdoing.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘My Lord, prison is more to my liking than that to which they invite me. And if You do not avert from me their plan, I might incline toward them and [thus] be of the ignorant.’”
islam.explanation: The prophet Joseph (Yusuf), threatened with prison unless he gives in to wrongdoing, prefers prison.
islam.tie_back: Yusuf is a precise image of the Kural’s ideal: facing real hardship, he still refuses the disgraceful act.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close match on choosing suffering over a shameful deed.

judaism.quote_or_event: Joseph, a slave in Potiphar’s house, refuses the repeated advances of his master’s wife, asking how he could do so great a wickedness and sin against God, and he is thrown into prison on her false charge.
judaism.explanation: Joseph’s refusal costs him his position and freedom, yet the Torah presents it as the root of his later rise.
judaism.tie_back: Joseph shows the Kural’s unshaken discernment: danger does not move him to a dishonourable act.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative parallel; paraphrased rather than quoted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada compares the wise to a rock that the winds of fortune cannot move.
buddhism.tie_back: The unshaken rock is a close image for the Kural’s naṭukku-aṟṟa kāṭci, vision that does not tremble.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Matches the steadiness half of the Kural; the verse does not speak directly of refusing base acts.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Bellerophon, a guest at the court of King Proetus, rejects the queen Anteia’s advances; she falsely accuses him, and he is sent to Lycia carrying a sealed message asking for his death, and made to face the Chimera and other perils.
greek_mythology.explanation: Bellerophon keeps his integrity even though it brings him into mortal danger, and he survives his trials.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s steady-minded person, he will not do the disgraceful thing even when refusing puts him in peril.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good narrative match; Homer tells the story briefly and without moral comment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates tells the jury that when the Thirty Tyrants ordered him and four others to arrest Leon of Salamis for execution, he alone went home and refused, though it might have cost him his life.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates says he cared nothing for death but everything about not doing anything unjust or unholy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a model case of the Kural: under real threat, a clear mind will not take part in a disgraceful act.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel of refusing a shameful act under political danger.

kurals.tamil:
எற்றென்று இரங்குவ செய்யற்க செய்வானேல்
மற்றன்ன செய்யாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Etrendru iranguva seyyarka seyvaanel
Matranna seyyaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: Do nothing that will later make you cry ‘What have I done!’; and if you have done such a thing, it is good not to do the like again.
kurals.elementary: If you ever do something that makes you think ‘Oh no, why did I do that?’, the best thing is to learn from it and never do it again. Even better is to stop and think first, so you don’t have to feel that way at all.
kurals.university: Eṟṟu eṉṟu is an exclamation of dismay (‘what is this!’), and iraṅkuva are deeds one will afterwards lament. The first line forbids such deeds, and the second deals with the case where one has already done one. Here the commentaries split. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read maṟṟu aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing such things again’, so repentance means not repeating the fault. The older reading, kept in the Drew-Lazarus prose explanation printed with Pope (‘it were good that he grieved not’) and in Puliyur Kesikan, takes aṉṉa ceyyāmai as ‘not doing that (grieving) again’: a minister should not waste himself in useless regret. This reading is usually traced to Parimelazhagar. The text also varies: ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net read செய்வானேல் (‘if he does’), while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints செய்வானேன், probably a typographical variant, since the conditional -ēl is needed for the sense.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Manu teaches that a person who has done a blameworthy deed, knowingly or not, and wishes to be freed from it, must not commit it a second time, and that the resolve ‘I will not do so again’ purifies him.
hinduism.explanation: In the Laws of Manu, the heart of expiation is sincere regret together with a firm resolve never to repeat the deed.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the majority reading of the second line: if one has erred, the good course is never to repeat it.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close to the Mu. Varadarasanar reading of the couplet; paraphrased.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus sends away the woman taken in adultery without condemning her, but tells her not to repeat the sin.
christianity.tie_back: This is the same two-step logic as the Kural’s second line: once a wrong is done, the good is never to do it again.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near match for the ‘do not repeat’ reading; the first line’s warning against regret-causing deeds is only implied.

islam.quote_or_event: “And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves [by transgression], remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins - and who can forgive sins except Allah? - and [who] do not persist in what they have done while they know.”
islam.explanation: The Quran praises those who, after doing wrong, turn back to God and do not persist in the wrong.
islam.tie_back: ‘Do not persist’ is exactly the Kural’s counsel after a regrettable deed.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the not-repeating reading.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides defines complete repentance as the sinner abandoning the sin, removing it from his thoughts and resolving never to do it again, so firmly that God can testify he will not return to it.
judaism.explanation: In the Laws of Repentance, the proof of teshuvah is facing the same situation and not repeating the sin.
judaism.tie_back: Maimonides spells out the Kural’s second line as a full theory of repentance.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a person commit evil, let him not do it again and again. Let him not find pleasure therein, for painful is the accumulation of evil.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada accepts that people may fall into wrong but insists they must not repeat it or take pleasure in it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is almost a word-for-word match for the second line of the Kural in its common reading.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match with the ‘do not do the like again’ interpretation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Sophocles’ play, Ajax, maddened by Athena, slaughters cattle believing them to be the Greek chiefs; on waking and seeing what he has done, he is overwhelmed with shame and despair.
greek_mythology.explanation: The tragedy dwells on the horror of recognising a deed that cannot be undone.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Ajax’s awakening is the ‘what have I done!’ moment that the Kural tells us to avoid by never acting that way to begin with.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Dramatises the regret the Kural warns of, but Ajax acted under divine madness and the play ends in suicide rather than amendment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza holds that repentance is not a virtue and does not arise from reason; one who repents of a deed is twice unhappy or weak, first in the deed and then in the sorrow.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, useless grief over past actions only adds a second weakness to the first.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the older commentarial reading of the second line, that a minister who has erred should not waste himself in grieving.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the minority ‘grieve not’ reading only; Spinoza argues from psychology, not statecraft.

kurals.tamil:
ஈன்றாள் பசிகாண்பான் ஆயினுஞ் செய்யற்க
சான்றோர் பழிக்கும் வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Eendraal pasikaanbaan aayinum seyyarka
Saandror pazhikkum vinai.
kurals.meaning: Even if you must watch your own mother go hungry, do not do what the wise condemn.
kurals.elementary: Suppose someone you love very much needs help. You would want to do anything for them, but stealing or lying still isn’t the right way. The Kural says even love for your own mother doesn’t make a wrong deed right. You must find an honest way to help.
kurals.university: This is the strongest statement in the chapter. Īṉṟāḷ, ‘she who bore (you)’, is the mother; pacikāṇpāṉ āyiṉum means ‘even if he should (have to) see her hunger’. Tamil ethics counts care of parents among the highest duties, so the verse deliberately picks the hardest case: not even that duty justifies deeds the cāṉṟōr (people of perfected character) condemn. Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators read the line without exception clauses, and Kalaignar sharpens it to ‘not even to relieve’ her suffering. This contrasts with the Sanskrit doctrine of āpad-dharma (law in emergencies), where the Mahabharata allows the sage Vishvamitra, in famine, to steal dog’s flesh to survive. The Kural here refuses that concession. The text is identical across sources apart from the sandhi form பசிகாண்பா னாயினுஞ் in thirukkural-thamizh.org. (Solomon Pappaiah’s printed gloss has பெற்றவனின், apparently a slip for பெற்றவளின்.)

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Kaikeyi demands Rama’s exile, his mother Kausalya begs him with tears to stay, yet Rama refuses to break his father’s pledged word, choosing dharma over his mother’s grief and his own claim to the throne.
hinduism.explanation: Rama feels his mother’s anguish deeply but holds that truth and duty cannot be given up even for her.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the epic makes a mother’s suffering the hardest test, and has dharma win.
hinduism.source: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda (Rama and Kausalya)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong emotional parallel with a mother’s distress set against dharma; Kausalya’s plea is grief, not hunger, and the deed refused is breaking a vow.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And not rather, (as we be slanderously reported, and as some affirm that we say,) Let us do evil, that good may come? whose damnation is just.”
christianity.explanation: Paul flatly rejects the idea that a good end can justify an evil act.
christianity.tie_back: This is the principle behind the Kural: not even the good of feeding one’s mother permits a condemned deed.
christianity._accuracy_note: Direct statement of the same ‘no evil means for good ends’ principle.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives.”
islam.explanation: The Quran requires justice even when it goes against one’s own parents and closest kin.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say that love for parents, however sacred, cannot override the demand of right action.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong parallel of duty to parents not overriding justice; the Quran’s setting is testimony, not hunger.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that for three sins, idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and murder, a person must let himself be killed rather than transgress, even to save his own life.
judaism.explanation: Although saving life normally overrides almost every commandment, the rabbis set limits that not even survival can cross.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Talmud names deeds so condemned that no desperate need, not even life, can justify them.
judaism._accuracy_note: Same absolute structure; the Talmud limits it to three cardinal sins, while the Kural covers every deed the wise condemn.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He is indeed virtuous, wise, and righteous who neither for his own sake nor for the sake of another (does any wrong), who does not crave for sons, wealth, or kingdom, and does not desire success by unjust means.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada defines the wise person as one who will not do wrong even on behalf of others.
buddhism.tie_back: ‘Nor for the sake of another’ is the principle of the Kural, which uses one’s own mother as the hardest example.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close match on refusing unjust means even for others.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded and starving on Thrinacia, Odysseus’ crew, urged on by Eurylochus, slaughter the forbidden cattle of Helios; Zeus wrecks their ship and all perish except Odysseus, who alone refused to eat.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hunger seemed to justify breaking a divine prohibition, but the forbidden meal destroyed those who ate it.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The episode shows the Kural’s point: dire hunger does not make a condemned deed safe or right.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match of starvation set against a forbidden act; the hunger is the crew’s own, not a mother’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates argues against Polus that doing wrong is worse than suffering it, so that if he had to choose, he would rather suffer injustice than commit it.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, wrongdoing harms the soul of the doer, which is a worse evil than any loss he could suffer.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural reaches the same conclusion: better to bear the pain of want than to do a deed the wise condemn.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close philosophical parallel; Socrates speaks of one’s own suffering, while the Kural uses a mother’s.

kurals.tamil:
பழிமலைந்து எய்திய ஆக்கத்தின் சான்றோர்
கழிநல் குரவே தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Pazhimalaindhu eydhiya aakkaththin saandror
Kazhinal kuravae thalai.
kurals.meaning: The deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained by taking on disgrace.
kurals.elementary: Would you rather have a small lunch you paid for honestly, or a big feast you got by cheating? The Kural says the small honest lunch is worth far more, because you can enjoy it with a clear heart.
kurals.university: Paḻi malaintu, ‘having taken on / worn blame’ (malai- as in wearing a garland), describes wealth won by accepting disgrace, and ākkattiṉ is the comparative ablative, ‘than such wealth’. Kaḻi nalkuravu is ‘extreme, excessive poverty’ (kaḻi = beyond measure). Parimelazhagar takes it as the poverty of the cāṉṟōr, and Mu. Varadarasanar adds that they accept it because they keep purity of action (viṉait-tūymai). Talai means ‘head, foremost’, so such poverty ranks first. The couplet restates 656 as a general value judgement and prepares for the fate of tainted wealth in 658-660. All three sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the sandhi forms மலைந் தெய்திய வாக்கத்திற்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna describes people of demonic nature who, bound by hundreds of desires and given to lust and anger, strive to pile up wealth by unjust means for their own enjoyment.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita counts gathering wealth through injustice (anyāyena artha-sañcaya) among the marks of a nature bound for ruin.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s tainted wealth is exactly the Gita’s wealth amassed by unjust means, which the wise would never choose over poverty.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match on condemning unjustly gained wealth; the Gita describes rather than compares it with poverty.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus asks what any gain could be worth if it costs the self.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural asks the same question in social terms: no fortune is worth one’s honour, so honest poverty is better.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match on the worthlessness of gain bought with inner loss.

islam.quote_or_event: “Say, ‘Not equal are the evil and the good, although the abundance of evil might impress you.’ So fear Allah, O you of understanding, that you may be successful.”
islam.explanation: The Quran warns believers not to be dazzled by the abundance of what is corrupt.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it ranks a little that is good above a great deal gained through wrong.
islam._accuracy_note: Close parallel on scarce good versus abundant evil.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Psalmist declares that the little a righteous man has is better than the great wealth of many wicked.
judaism.explanation: Psalm 37 comforts the upright, who may see the wicked prosper, with the promise that honest little is worth more.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the same comparison as the Kural: righteous poverty over wicked plenty.
judaism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; paraphrased rather than quoted.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Health is the most precious gain and contentment the greatest wealth. A trustworthy person is the best kinsman, Nibbana the highest bliss.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada redefines wealth as contentment, not as possessions.
buddhism.tie_back: The poverty of the good that the Kural praises is rich in the contentment and trustworthiness this verse values.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Only a partial match: it revalues wealth but does not address wealth gained through blame.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The poor, pious old couple Baucis and Philemon alone welcome Zeus and Hermes in disguise after their rich neighbours turn the gods away; the neighbours’ homes are flooded, and the couple’s hut becomes a temple.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid sets humble goodness against prosperous impiety, and the gods reward the poor couple.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural, the myth shows the poverty of the good as worth more than the wealth of the unworthy.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on virtuous poverty over unworthy wealth; the neighbours’ fault is inhospitality, not ill-gotten gain.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus says that if he can gain wealth while keeping himself modest, faithful and high-minded, he will; but if he must lose his own goods so that others may gain things that are not good, it is unjust and foolish to ask it.
philosophy.explanation: For the Stoic, integrity is a real good and money is not, so no trade of one for the other makes sense.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the Kural’s reasoning: better to stay poor than to exchange one’s good name for money.

kurals.tamil:
கடிந்த கடிந்தொரார் செய்தார்க்கு அவைதாம்
முடிந்தாலும் பீழை தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kadindha kadindhoraar seydhaarkku avaidhaam
Mudindhaalum peezhai tharum.
kurals.meaning: For those who do what the wise have forbidden instead of avoiding it, those deeds bring suffering even when they succeed.
kurals.elementary: If you sneak a cookie from the jar after being told not to, you might get the cookie, but then you feel worried and guilty, and you might get caught later. Even when a wrong plan ‘works’, it ends up making you unhappy.
kurals.university: The first line plays on the verb kaṭi- (‘forbid, reject’): kaṭinta, ‘things forbidden (by the great)’, and kaṭintu orār, ‘those who do not reject them and turn away’. Solomon Pappaiah specifies that such people act ‘thinking to gather wealth’, keeping the chapter’s focus on means of gain. The concessive muṭintālum, ‘even if they are accomplished’, is the point: success does not clean a forbidden act, which still brings pīḻai (suffering, affliction). Parimelazhagar’s tradition takes the suffering to come in this life as well as the next, through loss of reputation and later retribution. All sources agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org divides it as செய்தார்க் கவைதா / முடிந்தாலும்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Yama teaches Nachiketas that the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) are two different things; the wise choose the good, while the foolish choose the pleasant and fall short of the true goal.
hinduism.explanation: The Upanishad separates what gives immediate satisfaction from what is truly good, warning that success in the pleasant can be failure in the real aim.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s forbidden deed that ‘succeeds’ is a clear case of preyas won and śreyas lost.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Good conceptual match; the Upanishad’s aim is liberation rather than worldly consequence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb says what is gained by fraud tastes sweet at first but turns bitter and painful.
christianity.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point exactly: the wrong deed succeeds, and then brings grief.
christianity._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on success followed by suffering.

islam.quote_or_event: “So when they forgot that by which they had been reminded, We opened to them the doors of every [good] thing until, when they rejoiced in that which they were given, We seized them suddenly, and they were [then] in despair.”
islam.explanation: The Quran describes people who ignored warnings and prospered for a time, until their prosperity ended suddenly in ruin.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, success after ignoring what was forbidden only leads to a harder fall.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on apparent success preceding affliction; the verse concerns communities that rejected prophets.

judaism.quote_or_event: Proverbs says that treasures gained by a lying tongue are a vapour driven to and fro, and that those who seek them are seeking death.
judaism.explanation: Riches obtained by falsehood are pictured as a breath that vanishes and as a snare for the one who pursues them.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural too says a forbidden deed that gains its object still ends in suffering.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match; paraphrased from the JPS rendering.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So long as an evil deed has not ripened, the fool thinks it as sweet as honey. But when the evil deed ripens, the fool comes to grief.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada warns that the first sweetness of a wrong act hides the pain it will later bring.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same pattern as the Kural: the forbidden deed may succeed at first, but suffering follows.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: King Midas asks Dionysus that everything he touches turn to gold; the wish is granted, but his food and drink turn to metal, and he begs to be freed from the gift.
greek_mythology.explanation: Midas gets exactly what his greed asked for, and that success becomes his torment.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Midas is the Kural’s warning in myth form: a wrongly sought end, once achieved, brings suffering.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong image of success turning into suffering; Midas’s fault is greed, not a forbidden deed as such.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic, Socrates argues that the tyrant, who seems to have succeeded completely through injustice, is in truth the most wretched of men, enslaved to his desires and living in constant fear.
philosophy.explanation: Against Thrasymachus and Glaucon, Plato argues that injustice harms the one who does it, however well it seems to go.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural states the same idea briefly: wrongful deeds, even when they succeed, bring suffering to the doer.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close philosophical match on successful injustice as misery.

kurals.tamil:
அழக்கொண்ட எல்லாம் அழப்போம் இழப்பினும்
பிற்பயக்கும் நற்பா லவை.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhakkonda ellaam azhappoam izhappinum
Pirpayakkum narpaa lavai.
kurals.meaning: All that is taken by making others weep will go away and leave the taker weeping; what is gained by good means, even if lost for a while, bears fruit later.
kurals.elementary: If you take a toy by making another child cry, that toy will bring you trouble and tears in the end. But if you get something fairly and then lose it, good things will still come back to you later.
kurals.university: The first line hinges on the double use of aḻa, ‘so as to weep’: what was taken (koṇṭa) while making others weep will depart (pōm) making the taker weep. It is a compact statement of moral retribution. The second line balances it: naṟ-pālavai, ‘things of a good kind’, meaning wealth obtained by fair means, even if lost (iḻappiṉum), will give fruit afterwards (piṟ-payakkum). Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read this ‘fruit’ as a return of benefit in this life or merit in the next, and Kalaignar says such wealth ‘comes back again’. The verse sharpens the chapter’s theme of means into a law of consequences. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form அழக்கொண்ட வெல்லா மழப்போ மிழப்பினும் / பிற்பயக்கு நற்பா லவை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: At the rigged dice game the Kauravas win the Pandavas’ kingdom and drag Draupadi into the assembly in tears; her humiliation and curse are later repaid when the Kurukshetra war destroys the Kaurava line, and the Pandavas regain what they lost.
hinduism.explanation: Wealth and power taken through deceit and cruelty lead to the ruin of those who took them, while the wronged side is in the end restored.
hinduism.tie_back: The epic plays out both halves of the Kural: what is taken with tears goes with tears, and what is rightly held, though lost, returns.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva (the dice game) and its sequel
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match for both lines; summarised, not quoted.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.”
christianity.explanation: James warns rich oppressors that the cries of the workers they cheated have reached God, and that their hoarded riches will rot.
christianity.tie_back: The cries of the wronged, answered by the ruin of the wrongdoer, match the Kural’s ‘taken with tears, gone with tears’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong match for the first line; the second line’s promise is not in James.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allah destroys interest and gives increase for charities. And Allah does not like every sinning disbeliever.”
islam.explanation: The Quran teaches that gain from exploitation (ribā) will be wiped out, while wealth given away in good faith grows.
islam.tie_back: Both texts set two opposite laws side by side: exploitative gain vanishes, and rightly used wealth brings later increase.
islam._accuracy_note: Good two-part parallel; the Quran speaks of interest and charity specifically.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jeremiah compares the one who gets riches unjustly to a partridge that sits on eggs it did not lay: in the middle of his days the riches leave him, and at his end he is a fool.
judaism.explanation: The prophet’s image shows ill-gotten wealth deserting its holder before he can enjoy it.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the first line of the Kural: what was wrongly taken will not stay.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match for the first line; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Ill done is that action of doing which one repents later, and the fruit of which one, weeping, reaps with tears.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says a wrong action is known by the fruit it bears: the doer later reaps it in tears.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s play on weeping (aḻa) has a close echo in this verse’s ‘weeping, reaps with tears’.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong verbal and conceptual match to the first line; verse 68 gives the good counterpart.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hecuba, the Thracian king Polymestor murders the young Trojan prince Polydorus, entrusted to his care, to keep the boy’s gold; the grieving Hecuba lures him in, kills his sons and blinds him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Gold taken through a mother’s tears ends by bringing the same bereavement to its taker.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a vivid tragic version of the Kural’s first line: what is taken with tears goes with tears.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong narrative match of ill-gotten wealth repaid in grief; tragic revenge rather than a moral law.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lady Philosophy tells Boethius that the gifts of Fortune were never truly his, that she takes back what she gives, and that only goods of the mind cannot be taken away.
philosophy.explanation: Boethius separates outside goods, which always slip away, from inner goods, which last.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘good things’ that return after loss are close to Boethius’ goods that Fortune cannot take away.
philosophy.source: Boethius, The Consolation of Philosophy, Book 2
philosophy._accuracy_note: Loose match; Boethius is about the instability of all fortune, not just ill-gotten gain.

kurals.tamil:
சலத்தால் பொருள்செய்தே மார்த்தல் பசுமண்
கலத்துள்நீர் பெய்திரீஇ யற்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Salaththaal porulseydhe maarththal pasuman
Kalaththulneer peydhireei yatru.
kurals.meaning: Trying to secure oneself (or the state) with wealth gained through deceit is like pouring water into an unbaked clay pot and hoping to keep it.
kurals.elementary: If you pour water into a pot made of wet, unbaked clay, the pot softens and falls apart, and the water leaks away. Money gained by cheating is like that: it seems to hold for a moment, but it melts away and takes the ‘pot’ with it.
kurals.university: Calam means deceit or crooked means, and poruḷ ceytu ēmārttal (sandhi ceytē mārttal) is ‘to make wealth and guard/secure (with it)’, from ēmam, safety or protection. Parimelazhagar reads the verse in its ministerial setting: a minister who tries to protect his king and realm with wealth gained by fraud. This is why the prose explanation printed with Pope says ‘(For a minister) to protect (his king)’. The image is pacu-maṇ kalam, a pot of green, unfired clay: pouring water in and trying to keep it there (peytu irīi, with irīi an alapeṭai of iruttal, ‘to keep’) destroys both the water and the vessel. The metaphor makes the same point as the rest of the chapter: foul means undo themselves and ruin the very thing they were meant to protect. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree on the text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms சலத்தாற் … பசுமட் / கலத்துணீர்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Isha Upanishad opens by teaching that all this world is pervaded by the Lord, that one should enjoy it through renunciation, and that one must not covet anyone’s wealth.
hinduism.explanation: The verse bases right possession on non-grasping and forbids reaching for what belongs to others.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural shows what happens when that rule is broken: wealth grasped wrongly cannot be held.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shared prohibition on grasping at others’ wealth; the Upanishad has no image of such wealth dissolving.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And every one that heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them not, shall be likened unto a foolish man, which built his house upon the sand: And the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat upon that house; and it fell: and great was the fall of it.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus compares a life built without obedience to a house on sand that collapses when the waters come.
christianity.tie_back: Like the unbaked pot, the house on sand is a structure that fails the moment water tests it.
christianity._accuracy_note: Strong parallel image of a structure dissolved by water; the parable is about obedience generally, not ill-gotten wealth.

islam.quote_or_event: “O people, Allah is Good and He therefore, accepts only that which is good.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet teaches that God accepts nothing gained unlawfully, and describes a man whose food, drink and clothing are unlawful, asking how his prayer could be accepted.
islam.tie_back: Just as the Kural’s clay pot cannot hold water, the hadith says wealth from unlawful sources cannot support even prayer.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on the futility of wealth from impure sources; the hadith’s focus is acceptance by God.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Talmud rules that a commandment fulfilled through a transgression (mitzvah ha-ba’ah ba-aveirah), such as waving a stolen lulav on Sukkot, is invalid, citing Isaiah’s ‘I the Lord love justice, I hate robbery with a burnt offering’.
judaism.explanation: Even a sacred purpose cannot be achieved with stolen means; the tainted means cancel the act.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point in legal form: foul means ruin the very purpose they are meant to serve.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match on means corrupting ends; paraphrased.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Great Forty discourse the Buddha defines wrong livelihood as scheming, persuading, hinting, belittling and using gain to pursue gain, and teaches that right livelihood means abandoning these.
buddhism.explanation: Right livelihood (sammā-ājīva) is a limb of the Noble Eightfold Path, so earning by deceit is itself a departure from the path.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s calam (deceit) as a way of getting wealth is exactly what the Buddha calls wrong livelihood.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close match on deceitful earning; the sutta does not make the Kural’s point about such wealth failing to last.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod teaches that wealth should not be seized, since god-given wealth is far better; if a man takes great wealth by violence or by lying tongue, the gods easily bring him low, his house dwindles, and his wealth stays with him only a short time.
greek_mythology.explanation: The poet says ill-gotten riches are always unstable, because the gods undo them.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in Greek terms: wealth gathered by fraud will not stay, just as water will not stay in unbaked clay.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one thematic match; paraphrased rather than quoted.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle classes those who take from wrong sources, such as usurers, gamblers and robbers, as guilty of ‘sordid love of gain’ (aischrokerdeia), since they accept reproach for the sake of profit.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, where wealth comes from is itself a moral question, and gain bought with disgrace is a vice.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural condemns the same thing, wealth made by crooked means, and adds that it cannot last.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good match on condemning wrongly sourced wealth; Aristotle does not argue that such wealth is unstable.

ytamizh-ch66.title: Thirukkural Chapter 66: வினைத்தூய்மை / Purity in Action (with Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar commentaries)

thirukkuralnet-adhigaram66.title: வினைத்தூய்மை - அதிகாரம் 66 (with Puliyur Kesikan, Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi commentaries)

muslim-1015.title: Sahih Muslim 1015, The Book of Zakat: Acceptance of charity that comes from good (Tayyib) earnings

mn-117.title: Maha-cattarisaka Sutta: The Great Forty (MN 117), trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu
